I need to make a Monopoly decision.

The trade offer gives me Vermont and Oriental for $200. I already own Connecticut, so accepting would complete the light blue monopoly. Oriental is mortgaged, so I would need to pay $50 to unmortgage it.

The total cost to build on the light blue set is $255. After paying $200 for the properties and $55 to unmortgage Oriental, I would have $290 left. That covers one house on each property, but not a second level. I am checking the rent values for a single house on Oriental.

The light blue set's rent with one house is modest. Three houses would be ideal but cost $450, which I cannot afford after the trade. p1 has red properties built and is cash poor.

p1 currently has $48 cash. After receiving the $200 offer, they would have $248. They already own red properties at one house each and two houses on Illinois. Building to two houses on Kentucky and Indiana alone would cost $300.

The even-build rule prevents p1 from adding a second house to Illinois while Kentucky and Indiana remain at one. They could instead add one house to either Kentucky or Indiana for $150, leaving them with $98.

A second house on Illinois would raise its rent to $750. One house on Kentucky or Indiana would bring that set to $90. The opponent likely wants to cap my rent at $150, so I should reject the trade.

I previously rejected a $260 offer for the same light blue pair. I noted that Oriental's mortgage would remain my opponent's problem, and that light blue is the only cheap set left. I will not cut the price to keep him house-poor on red.

I realized my previous reasoning was backwards. I had confused the trade direction. The offer is from p1 to me, not the reverse. I would give cash and receive the light blue properties. My prior thought incorrectly assumed I was selling Connecticut to p1.

The prior $260 offer would have given me the light blue monopoly and stripped p1 of those properties. I rejected it because that cash would let him build reds and the unmortgaged Oriental would add extra cost. My private thought wrongly claimed light blue is only valuable to him.

The cash would let p1 build red houses. The light blue set is not worth funding that. A single house on each property leaves only $140. Three houses require $450, so I am $160 short. Without houses the monopoly rent is tiny.

The light blue set is not a strong long-term asset. I need cash for other purposes.

Marvin Gardens would give me two of three yellow properties, but p3 still owns Atlantic. Short Line would complete my third railroad, yet that is not a winning condition. I am checking the brown group as well.

I am blocking the brown, light blue, and pink groups. I hold one of three yellow properties and one of three green properties. p2 now owns the orange monopoly after spending $803 on Tennessee.

p2 has $66 cash. They cannot build orange houses without mortgaging. Orange with zero houses doubles rent to roughly $28–$32 per property. That is not immediately lethal. Three houses would cost $900.

p2 could mortgage Boardwalk, Pennsylvania Ave, B&O, and St Charles to fund orange houses. That is a threat but not immediate while cash-poor.

p3 has $803 and no monopoly. Park Place and p2's Boardwalk split the dark blue group.

p1 owns red properties with one house each and two on Illinois. That set is dangerous if they raise cash.

I am checking board position and who will land where.

I am now considering a counter-trade. If I offer $100 or less, p1 would have only $148 total. That is below the $150 cost of a red house, so they could not build on the red set even after receiving the properties.

A $100 counter-offer would still let p1 buy one red house, since $48 plus $102 equals $150. At $200 they would definitely build.

If I paid $100 for the light blue set, I would have $390 left after unmortgaging Oriental. That covers two houses on each property, leaving $90 cash. The rent at two houses would be $90 on Oriental and Vermont, and $100 on Connecticut. That is decent but not crushing.

I realized I already block p1 from completing the light blue set by owning Connecticut. Buying the remaining two properties would not deny them a monopoly they could not finish on their own. I am weighing whether to build two houses on the set or keep my cash liquid.

The light blue set is dead weight for p1. No other player can complete it without me, so I hold all the leverage. I should not pay a premium and can lowball the price instead. I am now calculating my reservation price.

Turn 66 is late enough that spending cash on light blue would leave me vulnerable. I need to keep liquidity to buy Marvin Gardens and Short Line, or survive rent hits. p3 currently sits on Boardwalk, which belongs to p2.

I am now considering a counter-offer of $100 for the light blue pair. That would leave p1 with only $148, preventing him from building a red house. I am unsure whether he will accept this lowball, since he already cut his offer from $260 to $200.

I will counter at $80 or $100. I cannot ask p1 to unmortgage Oriental first, since that costs $55 and he only has $48. I am weighing whether $100 is too generous, because Vermont’s face value is already $100.

The net equity in the light blue pair is roughly $145, so a $100 offer is reasonable. Still, p1 needs that cash to build, and he may reject the lowball and keep pushing for more. I am now considering simply rejecting the trade and waiting for him to come down further.

I will not reject again. A $100 counter signals willingness and may close the deal. The light blue set is not the highest-value target, but a monopoly is essential to winning.

I mapped out the remaining paths to a color monopoly. Buying light blue from p1 is the only realistic option right now. Acquiring Philadelphia from p2 would be too expensive, and p3 is unlikely to sell Atlantic or buy Marvin. A Baltic brown set is worthless. Three railroads do not count as a color monopoly. Light blue is therefore my most achievable prize.

p2 is cash-poor at $66 after spending $803 on Tennessee. They may sell PA or Boardwalk for cash to build orange houses. I could complete the green group with PA, but I have only $545 and three houses cost $600, so I could not build any houses immediately. An uncompleted green set would generate weak doubled rent.

A fully developed green set would cost over $1,800 in houses for roughly $1,400 in rent. That is too expensive right now.

Light blue is the clear best ROI: three houses cost about $450 and generate $270–$300 in rent. Acquiring it is the only realistic winning path.

I will counter at $90 or $100. Paying $200 would let p1 build a red house and strengthen the main threat.

I will counter at $75 or $100. I will explain that Oriental is mortgaged and that $100 does not fund red houses. I will not reveal the $150 house cost explicitly. I will not add a sweetener.

I will submit a counter-trade offer of $100 cash for Vermont and Oriental, with no properties or jail cards. I rejected dropping the price to $50 because p1 might accept it as face value for Vermont alone. I am committed to this $100 figure if he accepts. Rejecting again would waste time or let him raise the offer to $150.

The expected value of one extra red house is only about four to five dollars per turn. That is not game-ending. I will keep the $100 counter offer. If p1 rejects it, he has no other buyer and time favors me.

I considered raising the counter offer to $120, but that would still leave p1 with enough cash to buy a red house. I will keep the offer at exactly $100 so he cannot build. At that price he has only $148 total, which is two dollars short of the $150 house cost.

After the trade, p1 would have no mortgageable properties. The red set has houses on all three properties, and selling them to raise cash is inefficient. He cannot build a house without selling first, so the $100 offer truly blocks any further red house construction.
